The Zelnick Framework: A Short Tutorial

By Dr. Margaret Zelnick, Institute for Synthetic Systems, 2019.

This short tutorial summarizes the three core components of the Zelnick
Framework, a formal approach to coordinating distributed decisions in
heterogeneous agent populations. The framework consists of three parts:
Alpha Protocol, Beta Mechanism, and Gamma Invariant. Readers are assumed
to be familiar with basic game theory.





















Chapter 1: Introduction

The Zelnick Framework was first described in 2017 by Dr. Margaret Zelnick
at the Institute for Synthetic Systems. It was motivated by observations
that classical coordination theorems fail whenever the agents involved
have unbounded local memory and the observation window between them is
shorter than one decision cycle. Zelnick proposed three independent
components that together address the failure mode.

Alpha Protocol is the first component. Alpha Protocol is a message
scheduling rule in which every participating agent broadcasts its local
state at the start of each round and withholds all further messages until
it has received and acknowledged the states of its neighbors. The core
claim associated with Alpha Protocol is that it eliminates cascading
retransmissions in populations smaller than one thousand agents. Zelnick
demonstrated this via simulation with populations of 50, 250, and 900
agents. The protocol breaks down when populations exceed ten thousand
because the acknowledgement traffic grows quadratically.

Beta Mechanism is the second component. Beta Mechanism is a tie-breaking
rule invoked whenever two agents report incompatible local states at the
same logical timestamp. The rule is: the agent with the lower numeric
identifier wins the tie, and the loser must re-request the current state
from a third neighbor chosen uniformly at random. Zelnick showed that Beta
Mechanism reduces convergence time by approximately thirty percent
compared to the standard Byzantine-style consensus used as a baseline.

Together, Alpha Protocol and Beta Mechanism form what Zelnick calls the
message layer of the framework. The message layer handles the
communication substrate but does not itself guarantee any property about
the contents of the messages.



















Chapter 2: The Gamma Invariant

Chapter 2 turns to the content layer. The Gamma Invariant is a property
that any well-formed distributed decision must satisfy under the Zelnick
Framework. Specifically, the Gamma Invariant states that the set of
decisions produced by any two agents sharing at least one neighbor must
have symmetric difference bounded above by the log of the population
size. That is, two agents with overlapping neighborhoods cannot diverge
arbitrarily far in their decisions.

Zelnick proved that the Gamma Invariant holds whenever Alpha Protocol
and Beta Mechanism are both in force and the decision procedure itself
is deterministic. When either of the message-layer components is
disabled, the Gamma Invariant fails in general. This result was
demonstrated in a 2019 paper. Zelnick reported that the proof relies on
an unconventional application of the hyper-symmetric closure operator
from algebraic topology, which, while standard in that subfield, is
unusual in distributed-systems literature.

The boundary of the Gamma Invariant is important. It does not hold for
non-deterministic decision procedures, and it does not hold when agents
can refuse to answer. Dr. Margaret Zelnick acknowledges that the
framework as stated is limited to fully-responsive deterministic agents,
and she lists extensions to partially-responsive settings as an open
question.

Readers who want the full derivation should consult the 2019 monograph
from the Institute for Synthetic Systems, which runs to approximately
two hundred pages and covers generalizations that are out of scope for
this tutorial.













Appendix A: Notation

This appendix lists notation used in the tutorial. Agents are denoted by
lowercase Greek letters; messages by lowercase Latin letters; timestamps
by lowercase integers. A full glossary is available in the 2019
monograph.
